SVB held large amounts of long-duration, low-yield bonds whose market value fell sharply when interest rates rose. When depositors—many with uninsured balances—withdrew funds, the bank had to sell those bonds at a loss, crystallizing losses and weakening capital. That liquidity mismatch and concentrated deposit base made the run unmanageable despite the large portfolio.

SVB held long-term securities on a hold-to-maturity basis, and their market value fell significantly as the Federal Reserve raised interest rates, creating unrealized losses [D03-P01]. To raise cash for depositor withdrawals, SVB sold over $21 billion of securities, borrowed $15 billion, and planned an emergency stock sale [D03-P01][D04-P05]. The securities sale was at a large loss and, together with warnings from prominent investors, triggered a bank run in which customers withdrew $42 billion by the next day [D04-P01][D04-P05].
